summary: Extends IPv4 multicast addressing so that multicast addresses can be assigned together with unicast prefixes. Operators can then identify their multicast addresses without separate coordination.

eli5.summary: When a company gets its street addresses, it gets a block of group-broadcast addresses too. No separate request is needed.

questions: how does ubm differ from glop
subtitle: Give each organization IPv4 multicast addresses derived from its unicast prefix, with no allocation protocol.

tldr.problem: GLOP allocation of multicast addresses by AS number cannot work with 4-byte AS numbers and gives only 256 addresses per AS, which does not map well to organizations.
tldr.mechanism: Addresses in 234/8 embed the organization's unicast prefix after the leading 234, so whoever holds a /24 or shorter prefix gets matching multicast space.
tldr.outcome: Operators get multicast address space when they get unicast space, and anyone can find the holder by shifting the address left by 8 bits. The RFC says it does not obsolete GLOP.

today: RFC 6034 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this RFC, and it leaves RFC 3180 in force.

sections.title: Why Not GLOP
sections.content:
RFC 3180 defines GLOP in 233/8, embedding an AS number in the middle 16 bits of an IPv4 multicast address, giving 256 addresses per AS. Its disadvantages include that it cannot work with 4-byte AS numbers (RFC 4893), that an AS covering several organizations needs other mechanisms, that identifying the AS does not identify the right organization, and that only 256 addresses are automatic.

The IPv6 mechanism in RFC 3306 gives a multicast range to every subnet. This RFC specifies something similar for IPv4. It does not obsolete or update RFC 3180, which is still needed for prefixes more specific than /24.
sections.eli5: The old scheme tied addresses to big network numbers that were running out of room. This one ties them to street-address blocks instead.

sections.title: The Address Layout
sections.content:
A multicast address in 234/8 is a Unicast-Based Multicast (UBM) address. The remaining 24 bits hold the unicast prefix, starting at bit 8, followed by a group ID in the remaining bits. An organization with a /24 or shorter prefix appends its prefix to the /8 and may assign the remaining bits by any mechanism. Organizations with a prefix longer than /24 get no space from this mechanism.

The holder of a UBM address can be found by shifting the address left by 8 bits and looking up who owns the resulting unicast address. The embedded prefix MUST be a global unicast prefix, and UBM addresses MUST NOT be hard-coded in applications because global unicast addresses are not permanently assigned.

An AS gets more space than from GLOP if it has more than a /16 of unicast space, and less if it has less than a /16.
sections.eli5: Take the company's address block and put 234 in front. That is its own range of group addresses.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
An organization with 192.0.2.0/24 can use the multicast address 234.192.0.2 without coordinating with anyone. Shifting that address left by 8 bits gives 192.0.2.0, which reveals the holder.

An organization with a /16 such as x.y.0.0/16 can use 234.x.y.0/24 and assign addresses inside it by any mechanism it wishes.
sections.eli5: Put 234 in front of the company's address and you have a group address that is surely theirs.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The same intra-domain security techniques apply as with GLOP. When dynamic allocation is used within a prefix, the exposure to denial-of-service attacks may be reduced, because the area where nodes compete for addresses shrinks from an entire AS to an organization or less. IANA has assigned a /8 in the global IPv4 multicast address space for this purpose.
sections.eli5: Fewer neighbors fight over the same addresses, so there is less room for trouble. A whole block of 234 was set aside for this.
